amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **And where the ASV clefts a clause, the whole English frame goes the same way.** A cleft writes a dummy *it*, a copula, and a relative before the clause that carries the predication, and where the Hebrew writes a finite verb for that predication no morpheme answers to any of the three: the dummy and its copula are one `added` unit headed on the copula, and the cleft relative is its own `added` unit under rule 55, which marks a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause no written subordinator reaches. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **But an impersonal *it* the ASV writes inside one morpheme's own fixed English rendering is not such a dummy.** Where a Hebrew predicate word or interjection is rendered by an English expression the ASV never writes that word without — `רַע בְּעֵינֵי` → *it displease* and *it seem evil*, `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* — the *it* is part of that morpheme's own rendering, joins its unit and is never `added`, exactly as rule 30 gives the pronouns of `נָא` → *I beseech thee* to the particle and rule 55 gives the *As* of `חַי־אָנִי` → *As I live* to the adjective; rule 40 already reads `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* that way. Tell the two apart by the ASV's own use of the English, which is rule 31's test read for a frame rather than for a noun: where the ASV elsewhere writes that predicate's own word with nothing around it — *enough* for `רַב` — the frame is supplied and the preceding sentences govern, and where it never writes the word without the frame, the frame is the morpheme's. The unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme, so `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* heads on *Far*. This reaches a frame standing inside one morpheme's own rendering only: where every morpheme of the clause already holds its own English and the word is the opening of a cleft the ASV has built around it, the preceding sentences govern as before, and a referential subject pronoun answering to no morpheme at all is `added` on the terms rule 17 gives a supplied lexical subject noun. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **But an event of the subject's own is enough to make such a verb a supplied lexical one, and a participant the Hebrew does not write is not the condition.** Where the English verb names something the subject does, rather than asserting that the subject is, becomes or continues what the predicate says, it predicates an event the Hebrew never wrote and is `added` under the preceding sentences, however plainly the clause is verbless and whatever its predicate is made of — a prepositional predicate included, which rule 49 hands the construction's copula and nothing further. `נַפְשִׁי לַאדֹנָי` → *My soul* ***waiteth*** *for the Lord* leaves the *waiteth* `added` and gives the *for* to the `לְ`, while `לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ` → *his lovingkindness* ***endureth*** *for ever* keeps its verb with the `לְ` under rule 49, because enduring through the time the predicate names is the continuance a copula asserts and waiting for a person is not. Run the subtraction above by asking what a bare *is* written in that verb's place would leave the clause saying: where the bare copula says what the Hebrew says, the written verb is the construction's, and where an action goes missing with it, the verb is supplied. An ASV italic on such a verb corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **But the predicate morpheme that sentence looks for is one free to bear the copula, and a predicate that is itself a clause is not.** Where the predicate of such a tripartite clause is a relative or headless relative clause whose written finite verb already carries its own predication, no morpheme in it is available to take the matrix copula: assigning the word to that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses for the same reason in its matrix duration frame, and the resuming pronoun is then the clause's only overt anchor and takes the copula, exactly as an explicit subject does where the predicate is wholly elided. `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` → *That which hath been* ***is*** *that which shall be* gives *is* to `הוּא`, while `שֶׁ` keeps the *that which* rule 46's first rider gives it and `יִּהְיֶה` keeps its own *shall be*. Read what the predicate is before applying the preceding paragraph: a nominal, adjectival or prepositional predicate is free to take the copula and the pronoun is `unrepresented` as before, and one chapter may write both shapes, as ECC.1.9 and ECC.1.17 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: PSA.130.6 wrote a supplied verb where a copula would stand in a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate: `נַפְשִׁי לַאדֹנָי` → *My soul waiteth for the Lord*. Rule 20's test for telling a construction-supplied copula from a supplied lexical verb turns on whether the verb "adds no participant the Hebrew does not write", and *waiteth* adds none, so the test as written would admit it and rule 49 would then hand it to the `לְ`. The chapter marked it `added` on the strength of rule 34's *cheweth*, which is likewise an event with no added participant, and this amendment makes that reasoning explicit: an event of the subject's own is sufficient by itself, and a new participant is not required. The corpus is not disturbed — the 29 `לְ` → *endureth for* units keep their verb on the preposition, and the amendment says why, *endureth* being the continuance rule 20 already licenses under *remain* while *waiteth* names an action. Amendment rather than a new rule because the under-specified sentence sits inside rule 20 and a cross-reference would leave it standing for whoever reads it first.

conventions: The three `עִם` phrases of vv. 4 and 7 are read alike: each is its verbless clause's predicate and takes the construction-supplied copula, together with the presentative *there* where the ASV writes one (*there is with*, *with there is*, *with is*), while the single nominal of each clause — סְלִיחָה, חֶסֶד, פְּדוּת — is its subject and keeps only its own word. Rule 49's closing paragraph decides it, since the ASV writes no separate English subject in any of the three; the competing reading, which would put *there is* on the nominal and leave `עִם` a bare *with*, was named in each verse's notes and set aside.

Verse 6 carries three ASV italics and they are analysed three ways, by rule 7. *waiteth* is a supplied lexical verb for the verbless `נַפְשִׁי לַאדֹנָי` and *wait* is a supplied predicate for the gapped comparative colon; both answer to no morpheme and are `added` under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause and rule 34's boundary, and neither is folded into the `לְ` or into the participle rendered *watchmen*. The italic *more than* opening the third colon is not `added`: it is the one written `מִן`'s scope distributed over an asyndetic parallel member and joins that morpheme's discontinuous unit under rule 25. The supplied *Yea* standing beside it is `added` under rule 14, no conjunction morpheme standing anywhere in the verse.

amended.text: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **But an impersonal *it* the ASV writes inside one morpheme's own fixed English rendering is not such a dummy.** Where a Hebrew predicate word or interjection is rendered by an English expression the ASV never writes that word without — `רַע בְּעֵינֵי` → *it displease* and *it seem evil*, `חָלִילָה` → *Far be it* — the *it* is part of that morpheme's own rendering, joins its unit and is never `added`, exactly as rule 30 gives the pronouns of `נָא` → *I beseech thee* to the particle and rule 55 gives the *As* of `חַי־אָנִי` → *As I live* to the adjective; rule 40 already reads `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* that way. amended.why: PSA.130.6 wrote a supplied verb where a copula would stand in a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate: `נַפְשִׁי לַאדֹנָי` → *My soul waiteth for the Lord*. Rule 20's test for telling a construction-supplied copula from a supplied lexical verb turns on whether the verb "adds no participant the Hebrew does not write", and *waiteth* adds none, so the test as written would admit it and rule 49 would then hand it to the `לְ`. The chapter marked it `added` on the strength of rule 34's *cheweth*, which is likewise an event with no added participant, and this amendment makes that reasoning explicit: an event of the subject's own is sufficient by itself, and a new participant is not required. The corpus is not disturbed — the 29 `לְ` → *endureth for* units keep their verb on the preposition, and the amendment says why, *endureth* being the continuance rule 20 already licenses under *remain* while *waiteth* names an action. Amendment rather than a new rule because the under-specified sentence sits inside rule 20 and a cross-reference would leave it standing for whoever reads it first.

report: Checked all 13 candidate lemmas. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV wrote or by which morpheme stands in the clause: אֲדֹנָי is *Lord* (v2), *O Lord* (v3) and *the Lord* (v6) with the title suffix unrepresented in all three under rule 57; the two Sp1cs treatments in v6 are a possessive suffix on נֶפֶשׁ and the title suffix on אֲדֹנָי; the two הַ treatments are two assimilated articles the ASV writes *the* for (v6) against one it writes no *the* for (v7, rule 29); לְ is *To* (v2) and *in* (v5) because that is what the ASV wrote; כִּי is *But* (v4) and *For* (v7) on rule 14's open list; יִשְׂרָאֵל is a vocative in v7 and an object in v8. No split found.

Read the dump end to end for the split the lemma table cannot show — a supplied word marked `added` in one verse and folded into a morpheme in another. The supplied *for* of v5 *wait for Jehovah* goes to the verb because the Hebrew object is bare (rule 44), while v7's *in* goes to the written אֶל (rule 11); the supplied *the* of vv. 1, 2 and 6 always joins the noun (rule 15), and the article is unrepresented wherever no *the* is written (vv. 1, 4, 7); the copula goes to the preposition in all three עִם clauses (vv. 4, 7). Consistent.

Verse 6's three ASV italics are analysed three ways, and that is deliberate rather than a lapse: *waiteth* and *wait* answer to no morpheme and are `added`, while the italic *more than* of the third colon is the written מִן's scope distributed over an asyndetic parallel member under rule 25. Rule 7 governs — the markup is evidence, not a label. Recorded as a convention.

BSB disagreements: all seven are documented convention differences, none an error. Three are the 1cs suffix of אֲדֹנָי, which rule 57 marks unrepresented because the ASV writes no possessive anywhere in the title (vv. 2, 3, 6); one is the paragogic he of שִׁמְעָה (rule 32); one is the בְ of בְקוֹלִי, whose object the ASV promotes to a bare direct object, *hear my voice* (rule 40); two are articles for which the ASV writes no *the*, הַסְּלִיחָה and הַחֶסֶד (rule 29).

One amendment returned, to rule 20. The chapter's *waiteth* is a supplied verb standing where a copula would stand in a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate, and rule 20's present test — a linking verb "adds no participant the Hebrew does not write" — would wrongly admit it, since it adds no participant either. The amendment makes an event of the subject's own sufficient by itself, and keeps the corpus's 29 `לְ` → *endureth for* units on the preposition by saying why continuance is a copula and waiting is not.
